In {n} Paul Morphy watched an opera in Paris, and between the acts he played two noblemen together. They played slowly and passively, moving the same pieces again and again. Morphy did the opposite: every move brought a new piece into play. When their king was still in the centre, he sacrificed a knight, then a rook, then his queen. With only a bishop and a rook left, he gave checkmate. Lesson: fast development beats extra material.

In {n}, {n}-year-old Bobby Fischer played a strong master, Donald Byrne. On move {n} Fischer let his queen be taken. In return he got a rook, two bishops and a pawn, and his pieces worked like a team. A "windmill" of knight checks won even more, and he finished with mate. It was called "The Game of the Century". Lesson: count the whole position, not just the queen.
